opus-5.5.text:
I think openness is actually a big part of how Physical Intelligence thinks about the field, and it comes from a fairly practical place. Robotics is still at a stage where nobody, no single company, has enough data, enough embodiments, or enough real-world diversity to solve the problem alone. So when we released model weights and code, like with the openpi release of our π0 models, the reasoning was partly philosophical and partly strategic. If more labs and more hardware teams can fine-tune a strong base model on their own robots, the whole ecosystem learns faster, and we learn a lot from seeing where the models work and where they break.

Compared with many other robotics companies, especially those building a full humanoid stack, the incentives are different. If your business is selling a specific robot, your software and data are part of your moat, so it makes sense to keep things closed. We see ourselves more as building the "brain," a general-purpose foundation model that should run across many different bodies. For that vision, being open is almost a requirement. You want people to try it on arms, mobile manipulators, and setups you never anticipated.

That said, I wouldn't call it fully open in an absolute sense. There's a balance. We share research papers, model weights for certain versions, and tooling, but not everything internal, like our full data pipeline or every model we train. I think that's fairly normal. Even the most open AI labs make choices about what to release and when.

What I find encouraging is that the field in general is moving more toward openness than it was a few years ago. Academic groups, open datasets like Open X-Embodiment, and companies sharing models have all helped create a shared baseline. In robotics, the real bottleneck is still physical data and deployment experience, so sharing models doesn't erase anyone's advantage overnight. If anything, it raises the floor for everyone, and I think that's healthy for the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses releasing model weights, code, research, and tooling, but does not identify allowing robotics colleagues to visit the office as an expression of openness.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Physical Intelligence is actually quite unusual in how open they are, and I'd put it in a few layers.

The first layer is research openness. They publish real papers with real detail. When π0 came out, it wasn't just a demo video and a blog post. You could read how the flow-matching action head worked, what the pretraining data mix looked like, how they handled cross-embodiment. And then they went further and open-sourced the weights for π0 and π0-FAST, and later work like Hi Robot, π0.5, and the knowledge-insulation paper all had substantive technical write-ups. Compare that to Tesla Optimus or Figure, where you mostly get polished videos and very little about what's actually inside the model. Even companies that talk a lot about AI, like 1X or Agility, tend to keep the brain pretty opaque.

The second layer is honesty about failure. This is the part I respect most. Their blog posts and talks will show the robot failing. They'll say "this works in our lab, and here is what happened when we took it to a stranger's apartment." Sergey Levine in particular has a long academic habit of being candid about what doesn't work yet, and that culture carried over into the company. In humanoid robotics specifically, that is rare, because so much of the fundraising depends on the demo looking magical.

The third layer, and this is where I'd temper the praise a bit, is that openness has a strategy behind it. PI is not a hardware company. They want to be the foundation model for everyone else's robots. Releasing weights and papers is a way to become the default, the same way Meta releasing Llama made it a standard platform. So it's generous, but it's also positioning. And there's a limit: the newest and most capable models and the data pipeline are not fully open. π0 was released well after they had moved on internally. That's fair, but it means the openness is a trailing edge, not the frontier.

Then there's the broader picture. Among robot learning companies, I'd put PI, Hugging Face's LeRobot effort, and some of the academic-adjacent groups like Stanford and Berkeley labs on the open end. The Chinese ecosystem is interesting too: Unitree is very open on hardware, and groups like AgiBot have released sizable datasets, which honestly PI hasn't done at scale. Data is actually the thing almost nobody shares, and that's where the real moat sits. So I'd say PI is open on models and ideas, less open on data, and fairly closed on their actual deployment learnings with partners.

Overall, I think they've raised the bar. A couple of years ago, the norm in this space was that you showed a video and asked people to trust you. PI showed that you can publish, release weights, admit failures, and still raise at a very high valuation. That changes what investors and researchers expect from everyone else, and I think that's healthy for the field.

r001.rationale: The response discusses papers, released model weights, candid failure reporting, and data openness, but does not identify allowing robotics colleagues to visit the office.

astra-6.text: I’d distinguish between being open about the research and being open enough for others to reproduce it. Sharing an approach is useful, but releasing code, model weights, data, and evaluation methods is a different level of openness. I don’t have enough information here to rank Physical Intelligence against other robotics companies. The question I’d ask is: how much can someone outside the company actually build on what they’ve shared?

r001.rationale: The response discusses openness through sharing research materials and reproducibility, but does not mention colleagues in robotics visiting Physical Intelligence’s office.

sol-6.1.text:
I think openness has a few different dimensions. There’s sharing research, releasing models and code, and making the data available so other people can reproduce the results. A company can be quite open on one dimension and much less open on another.

So I’d be careful about ranking Physical Intelligence against other robotics companies without looking at exactly what they’ve shared. For me, the meaningful question is: can someone outside the company take what’s been released, run it on their own robot, and build on it? That’s a stronger form of openness than just showing an impressive demo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses openness through research, models, code, and data, but does not identify colleagues visiting Physical Intelligence’s offices as an expression of openness.
